# Title Cap and Credential Migration Notes

This round of checks no longer tries to establish the full relationship between two behaviors from a single old filename. The old investigation records do lead from the issue names and call names to `web/src/locales/en.ts`, and that entry point is still useful: whoever takes over can use the names from that time to return to the existing TypeScript module, then inspect the references in that revision. It is not proof of where title splitting or credential resolution belongs.

The earliest records combined the two items for a simple reason: both appeared in the compatibility wrap-up for R6.4.0, and both old descriptions were very short. That approach left behind a misleading habit—find a shared file first, then use the same set of examples to explain both issues. During actual review, title examples and entry points that trigger credential behavior cannot substitute for each other. The old records are retained as a recovery entry point; the new checks split into two tracks here.

```text
Old records
  Issue name / Call name
          |
          v
web/src/locales/en.ts
          |
          +-- Previously treated as a shared entry point for checks

Current records
  Lossless title token cap
          |
          v
  Failure text or output bytes --> Example review

  Shared credential resolution
          |
          v
  Existing tests or examples --> User-path gaps
```

## Purpose of the Old Entry Point

The old approach was to follow an issue name into `web/src/locales/en.ts`, then put title tokens and shared credentials into the same batch of check items after seeing the relevant names. This entry point is still valid, but it only answers "where to continue looking." It cannot answer exactly which boundary changed the title content, nor can it show whether a test or example actually triggered the shared credential path.

There is another practical reason to retain the old entry point: the wording in early material may not be precise enough, but the issue names and call names remain clues for finding the context from that time. The migration records do not need to rewrite this old material to look like documentation of the current implementation. When the early investigation needs to be recovered, the original names can still be used to return to that path; if the current references do not connect, simply record the break rather than inventing module ownership or a call sequence.

Previously, "both names can be traced back through the old entry point" was treated as a reason to share validation material. That judgment no longer applies. Being able to locate the names only means the old records still have navigational value; it does not mean the two compatibility behaviors have the same inputs, the same failure symptoms, or the same fix location.

The column in the old table that records the title issue as "validate together with credentials" remains in the archive, but is no longer used for release decisions. It can remind future team members why the two tracks were once mixed together, but it can no longer serve as a status summary. Every status in the new records must trace back to its own example or triggering entry point.

## Title Tokens: Recover Boundary Examples First

The migration subject for Lossless title token cap is boundary examples, not an abstract statement that "the title is too long." First retrieve the original content from the old records that can demonstrate the issue. The work item on card ARG-209 requires preserving the current failure text or output bytes when adding repository tests; this material should stay with the example and must not be condensed to "reproduction failed" during cleanup.

The first step for title examples is not to judge the implementation, but to confirm whether comparable original content is available. If the old records contain only an issue name and no complete example, record the example as missing. Do not fill the gap with another short title, a similar title, or a description written later on the fly, because these cannot show what happened at the original boundary.

Once an example is obtained, save the original failure text or output bytes. What is saved here is not a summary written after reading it, but content that can be compared repeatedly during later reviews. A title still looking readable does not mean the original content did not change at the boundary; a difference in the presentation layer also cannot be attributed directly to the token limit. The failure text or output bytes ensure that later tracing has at least the same object to compare.

If the example comes from a test added later, keep it separate from the original description in the old records. An added test can help hold the example, but it cannot retroactively prove that the old records already had the same coverage at the time. Continue to state what is missing from the old material rather than using a new example to overwrite its historical context.

When tracing references, simply continue from the old issue names and call names in `web/src/locales/en.ts`. This step is only for locating them: confirm that the names in the old records still lead to a place that can be inspected. It is not used to assert that the title behavior must be implemented by that module, nor does it substitute a file location for the example itself.

The status of the title track on this page can be maintained as follows:

- An old example exists, and its failure text or output bytes have been retained: treat it as an example pending review and continue inspecting the current references.
- An old example exists, but the original failure material is missing: retain the example's source and mark what is missing; do not fill in the content from memory.
- No complete example exists: retain the old issue name and a note that the example is missing; do not substitute a similar title.
- A later test can hold the example: treat the test as a supplementary entry point while preserving the distinction between the old description and the test material.

These states must not be collapsed into two broad labels, "title confirmed" or "title unconfirmed." For migration, whether the missing piece is original content, a way to incorporate it into a test, or the current reference location determines what needs to be added next. Clearly documenting the gaps also avoids having to infer the background again from short phrases during the next release check.

When recovering the old path, the title track recovers the old issue name and the original content that was saved. If the new examples have not been fully organized, unverified explanations must not be written back into the old material. Even if the test entry points are adjusted later, the original boundary behavior should remain in the records rather than disappearing along with changes to test organization.

ARG-209 has moved from handoff confirmation into active work. That card is suitable for continuing to collect the failure material needed for repository tests; this page retains only the migration relationship along this track, from the old entry point and original examples to their inclusion in tests. Progress on the card does not replace the examples themselves, nor does it automatically fill in missing output content.

## Shared Credentials: Start with the Triggering Entry Point

Records for Shared credential resolution start with an entry point that can trigger the behavior, not with a set of hypothetical provider combinations. ARG-226 requires using existing tests or examples to trigger this path and writing user paths that are not yet covered back to the card. This is the extent of what the current material supports: first confirm whether the existing entry point reaches the target behavior, then record the entry points that are not covered.

In practice, first choose one existing test or example. Record whether it is a test or an example, and whether it can demonstrate that shared credentials are resolved. Do not assume the resolution path has been traversed just because credential-related fields appear in the input; the presence of configuration and the triggering of a path are two different things.

When an entry point can trigger the behavior, the focus of the record is the entry point type and the scope it covers. A test entry point and an example entry point must not be merged into a single "tested path": whether the former can reach the behavior does not automatically establish the user usage pattern represented by the example; the latter being able to show configuration also does not automatically establish that existing tests cover the same path.

When an entry point cannot trigger the behavior, simply record "not triggered" and the entry point name. This is more helpful for continuing the investigation later than adding a paragraph of speculation about the internal resolution process. In this case, do not record the presence of configuration as compatibility complete, and do not interpret the lack of a trigger as necessarily an implementation issue; what needs to be retained now is an entry point that can be tried again and the gap it leaves.

List user-path gaps separately. A test being able to trigger the behavior does not automatically cover user entry points, and an example being able to show configuration does not automatically cover test paths. If either is not yet covered, Shared credential resolution still has a gap. This round does not require enumerating all compatibility cases first; the focus is on retaining triggering entry points that can be investigated further and explicitly identifying uncovered paths.

The credential track is recovered differently from the title track. The title track recovers original examples and failure material; the credential track recovers test or example entry points and the user-path gaps recorded at the time. If an entry point is later renamed or moved, the old records should still preserve whether it was originally a test or an example, to avoid mixing the two types of entry point into a "tested path" that cannot be reviewed.

ARG-226 is the tracking entry point for the shared credential path. Write the trigger results from existing tests or examples and the uncovered user paths back to that card, rather than duplicating the card's handling process on this page. This page retains what material should be carried through the migration: entry point category, triggered or not-triggered status, and user paths that are not yet covered.

## Stopping Points When Returning to Release Checks

The two tracks can appear side by side in release checks, but their evidence must not be merged again. The title track centers on examples, and the credential track centers on triggering entry points; the migration state this page requires preserving is one in which both sides can still be traced back. A shared release date is not a reason to mix their material together.

| Current state | Material to retain | Judgments that must not be substituted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A title example exists but has not yet been incorporated into a test | Failure text or output bytes, old issue name | Do not mark the example as passed |
| A title example is missing | Note that the example is missing, old entry point | Do not substitute a similar title |
| A credential test or example can trigger the behavior | Entry point type, trigger record | Do not extrapolate to user paths that are not explicitly documented |
| A credential entry point did not trigger the behavior | Entry point name, not-triggered status | Do not treat the presence of configuration as compatibility complete |

Before release checks, the title track checks whether the original failure text or output bytes and a corresponding example are available; the credential track checks whether there is a test or example that can trigger the behavior, or an explicitly recorded not-triggered status and user-path gaps. If any item is missing, retain the gap rather than filling it with material from the other track.

DOC-23 records another set of validation designs involving Wiki document identity and Provider credential compatibility. It can serve as a related reading entry point, but the objects in it must not replace the title examples or shared credential gaps on this page. Both pages appearing in the checks for R6.4.0 does not mean they share the same migration evidence.

The old shared checklist can remain archived to help people understand the original organization; it is no longer used to close out the two tracks. Title examples need to return to the original content, and credential compatibility needs to return to actual entry points. This way, even if references, tests, or examples change later, the next review will still know which type of material to continue from.

Its actual adjacency to `accepts`, `scalar`, and `values` must be found.

Option A is to accept legacy inputs and convert them to a canonical list at one boundary. A scalar is wrapped only once, at the entry point, and subsequent processing keeps the ordered-list approach. This centralizes sorting and empty-value checks, but if a caller depends on the original scalar, the migration will change the shape it receives. Option B is to skip unified conversion, retain scalars and lists separately, and have each usage site continue to distinguish `lists` from a single value. This is less disruptive to old code, but every usage site has to know about differences in source count, and there will be no single place to check if a third shape appears later.

Do not record A as the decided approach yet. We need at least one actual call or test output for each of the following: a single source, multiple sources, an empty `values`, and a change in order. If calls in the repository only use single values, forcing lists would actually expand the scope of changes. If review finds that `source_chunk_id` exists only in a legacy adapter layer, the migration should target that layer rather than all consumers of `wiki_claim_chunk_ids`. ARG-212 can serve as a navigation starting point for Claim source identifier shapes, but cannot replace evidence from these calls.

## Where to Handle Model Aliases

The options for where to perform Model-type alias normalization are clearer: first, convert aliases to canonical types during model discovery or configuration parsing; second, retain the original value until selected-model verification and recognize aliases in the compatibility check. The first approach means later checks handle only one identifier, at the cost of requiring discovery to know all aliases. The second preserves the original input, at the cost of potentially showing different names in verification, logs, and failure output.

No specific aliases have been finalized, and there is no failure output we can cite, so we will not invent a mapping table. The question to investigate is not "which name is more standard," but where the most recent report obtained the model type, which checkpoint rejected or accepted it, and whether the user ultimately saw a discovery failure or a verification failure. ARG-229 only provides navigation for Model-type alias normalization. If the actual call occurs before verification, try option one first; if the alias comes from external configuration and needs to be echoed back unchanged, then evaluate option two.

## Tentative Boundaries After Review

Do not combine these two issues into one universal converter. Claim source identifiers concern the shapes of single values and ordered collections; model aliases concern mapping names to compatible types. They can be discussed in the same interface review, but their migrations and rollbacks should be recorded separately. The recommendation is to start with a read-only review: follow file references to find the entry point for `accepts`, retain one raw input sample, then check whether `wiki_claim_chunk_ids` and the model type check really go through the same call chain.

If unified Claim conversion introduces shape incompatibility in existing calls, roll back only the boundary conversion and retain the original identifiers. If model alias conversion prevents selected-model verification from recognizing old names, restore the path that preserves the original value before verification. Neither rollback can be deemed complete based on the top of the file alone. The outstanding items remain the actual calling patterns, failure or success output, affected callers, and whether there is already legacy data that needs migration.

This troubleshooting page did not grow from a stable entry point. The earliest index grouped issue terms, filenames, and several symbols together; later records put chunking results and model verification near the same card. In actual handling, first separate the reports; otherwise, halfway through the investigation it is easy to mistake a path for behavior and a local result for the result of the entire issue.

## What Has Been Confirmed at the File Level

The entry file is `rag/advanced_rag/knowlege_compile/wiki.py`. The file header that could be directly seen at the time was:

```python
import asyncio
import json
import logging
import re
```

These four dependencies indicate the file's local neighborhood. The old investigation also left search terms such as `knowledge`, `chunk`, `chunk_hash`, `produces`, `same`, `stable`, `content`, `hash`, `identical`, `wiki`, `pipeline`, and so on. Search terms can lead someone to a file; they cannot answer "who calls whom" on behalf of the file.

Therefore, the first step is only to verify the entry: confirm the path, confirm the revision being investigated, and save the matched symbols. If there are still only a path and symbols, do not write the file location as the execution location, and do not interpret terms such as `produces` or `identical` as results that have already occurred.

## Branching by Observed Symptoms

```text
Report received
├─ Concerns chunking results
│  ├─ Contains chunk and content
│  │  ├─ First confirm whether both came from the same processing run
│  │  ├─ Then save the corresponding hash records side by side
│  │  └─ If only one side is present, stop at incomplete evidence
│  ├─ Says "the content is the same but the results differ"
│  │  ├─ Return to the references for that revision
│  │  ├─ Find the direct object that produces the hash
│  │  └─ If the call edge cannot be found, record only the observation
│  └─ Contains only an issue title, screenshot, or retelling
│     └─ Mark it as pending review; do not close it with same, stable, or identical
└─ Concerns verification of the selected model
   ├─ Has a clear public entry point
   │  ├─ Run through this entry point
   │  ├─ Save the complete returned content
   │  └─ If there is an exception, save it together with the exception text and location
   ├─ Has only the selected model name
   │  └─ Stop at unverified
   └─ The entry point and file path do not match
      └─ Keep the entry point and path separately, and trace the references again
```

The stopping points differ between the two branches. On the chunking side, it must be possible to place `chunk`, `content`, and the corresponding `hash` back into the same input context; on the model side, it must be possible to associate the return or exception with the actually selected model and the public entry point. If only one side is satisfied, the other side remains unconfirmed.

## Conclusions Left by the Old Page

The early version placed `chunk`, `content`, `hash`, `same`, `stable`, and `identical` in a sequence. This made searching faster, but the risk of turning "looks the same" into "already stable" is also embedded in that sequence of terms. This old judgment is retained because it explains why this page was repeatedly referenced; it is not the later final conclusion. Looking at the file again or rereading the content only adds locating material; it does not automatically add execution evidence.

If there is only a file path, record "entry point found." If a piece of output is obtained but it cannot be shown to correspond to the same chunk input, stop here anyway. If there is only an old link or screenshot, retain the original and do not turn the screenshot text into a return value. When there is no actual return, exception, or corresponding call material, do not fill in the result seen by the user.

## Time Gaps in the Records

After the baseline record for ARG-213, one unresolved field note remained. The original record emphasized that one point in Deterministic chunk hashing was still unconfirmed; continue only with the current segment and leave the open item open. When investigating ARG-213, retain this statement together with the object currently found. It indicates that the verification scope was limited at the time; it does not indicate that the entire chunking flow produced the same result, nor that the call form of the user entry point has been recovered.

ARG-230 later entered the work record. Its requirement is narrower than the title: run Selected-model verification compatibility through the current public entry point, and record only what this path actually returns or throws. Here, the entry point belongs to the context of that work record. An old screenshot, model name, filename, and a seemingly related exception cannot substitute for one another. If no return or exception can be found, leaving the entry point and the gap is sufficient; do not derive compatibility from a name just to give the branch a conclusion.

Although these two tasks appear on the same page, they cannot borrow results from each other. A return value from the model verification path does not close the chunk_hash unconfirmed item in ARG-213; finding the same content on the chunking path does not close the selected model verification in ARG-230. When both names appear in a report, first place the two sets of objects in separate columns, and save the inputs, paths, and results separately.

## Recovery Actions That Have Failed

The old investigation usually proceeded in the order "recheck the file, recheck the content, then check the hash." This order can still be used for locating things, but the output of each step must be kept separate: file inspection produces paths and symbols, content inspection produces input records, and hash inspection produces the corresponding values. When the three do not fall within the same execution record, they cannot be combined into a successful recheck.

Another easy-to-make erroneous merge is to first find `wiki` or `pipeline`, then use the adjacent `produces` to infer the generated object; or to see `same` and `stable` and treat the text as output. This approach once left a convenient index in the old page, but it did not resolve the call boundary. During cleanup, remove only the inferences, not these search terms, because they can still help locate historical pages.

If reopening the revision yields only pointers from the old investigation, leave the revision, file path, and matched symbols, then stop. If output exists but has no correspondence to the same chunk, content, or selected model, stop as well. If the recheck covers only the current segment of ARG-213, or only the public entry point of ARG-230, the entire item likewise cannot be marked as resolved.

## Stop Conditions and What to Leave Behind

Stop this investigation when any of the following conditions is met:

- There is only `rag/advanced_rag/knowlege_compile/wiki.py`, with no reference relationships for that revision;
- There is only an issue name, old link, screenshot, or retelling, with no original returned content;
- There is output, but it cannot be associated with a chunk, content, or selected model;
- The result covers only the current segment of ARG-213, or only the public entry point of ARG-230;
- Both reports appear, but there is no evidence that they share the same execution object.

When stopping, leave the paths found, the original objects, the matched symbols, and the unconfirmed items. Do not write "the content looks the same" as a stability conclusion, and do not write the absence of a thrown exception as a compatibility conclusion. ARG-213 and ARG-230 are only navigation entry points for this page; the Incremental chunk-state delta in DOC-27 is adjacent material and cannot be used to fill this page's gap.

### Old Index (Retained)

`knowledge → chunk → hash → wiki pipeline` is still used by some people to search for the page. It is a search lead, not an implementation ownership statement. The file-header dependencies are also only leads at the same level. The historical judgment, partial rechecks, and open items left later were not fully merged, so the old terms and old paths are retained.

versions.body:
# Topic Evidence Query Decision

This record preserves a narrowly scoped decision about Evidence-rich topic queries during R6.4.0. The old draft was not taken down, not because its reasoning later became more complete, but because it explains why the investigation was initially directed toward the query code: at the time, there were only descriptions along the lines of "inconsistent results in the user's environment," with no paired results and no samples sufficient to separate topics, evidence, and input conditions.

"Query side" on this page is not a precise module name. It was a phrase used at the time to narrow the investigation scope: start by looking at the visible text returned by topic queries. This wording was later read more strongly than intended, as though evidence text were inherently the query layer's responsibility; the original decision had no such proof, but it was not rewritten at the time either.

The initially recorded problem had two sides. In one call, the topic and evidence appeared to be linked; in another call, the topic was still recognizable, but the evidence portion could not be confirmed on that basis. The two phenomena were recorded side by side, but the original inputs, document state, and output order were not saved. Thus, "the same type of query" was only a classification made in the user's environment, not a verified instance of the same request.

The working assumption at the time was that the topic query had already done the main work, and the remaining instability occurred when topic hits were assembled into text containing evidence. This assumption fit the description "the topic is still there, but the evidence looks different," and also made it convenient to set aside cases where the topic could not be found at all. Its weakness was equally clear: without samples, the supposedly remaining topic could be the same topic, a related topic, or merely similar wording.

The earliest decision remained: first inspect where the visible results originate near the topic query, then decide whether to expand the scope to evidence, claim source identifier, and document identity. This sequence controlled the initial reading scope; it did not commit to a final attribution, nor did it rule out differences caused by call inputs or document state.

## Explanations Considered Together at the Time

**Different topic-term matching.** If one result has no topic and another does, the subsequent evidence text is only a surface symptom. This explanation can account for completely different topic results, but cannot by itself explain descriptions where the topic remains recognizable while the evidence portion changes. The initial draft still put it first in the investigation order, because the issue was initially presented as a topic query issue, and there was no material proving that topic hits were already stable.

**Different text assembly after a topic hit.** This was the explanation the initial draft actually favored. It allows the topic to remain in the results while the evidence-rich portion changes between the two results. The cost is that we must know which objects connect the topic and evidence; at the time, no objects were retained for item-by-item comparison, and the visible text was not saved either. The old draft deferred this gap instead of treating it as a prerequisite for maintaining the judgment.

**Different call conditions.** This was the broadest explanation. If the two calls did not have the same inputs, or did not operate against the same document state, inferring query logic from output differences would lose its basis. The initial draft acknowledged this possibility, but did not make comparison of inputs and document identity a checkpoint; this made "query side first" look sufficient to rule out the other two explanations.

The three explanations were not fully distinguished at the time. The investigation order ultimately retained was to first read around the topic query, then return to the evidence text and object relationships if that did not explain the issue. The benefit of this order was a narrow entry point; its cost was treating call conditions as background rather than as part of the conclusion.

## The Old Classification

The initial draft used the following two rows to separate the descriptions from the user's environment:

| Text seen at the time | Initial draft classification | Action taken at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The topic itself did not appear | No topic query hit | First inspect the topic terms and returned text |
| The topic still appeared, but the evidence portion differed | Inconsistent evidence-rich representation | First inspect the assembly process near the topic |

This table later became easy to treat as a localization rule. Its original intent was only to record the classification approach: it did not state that "the topic appears" was sufficient to prove a topic hit, nor that "the evidence portion differs" necessarily resulted from evidence assembly. Display position, truncation, call conditions, and document state could all produce similar phenomena. The initial draft did not include these counterexamples in the table, so the table conveyed more certainty than the material available at the time justified.

During the discussion, Evidence-rich topic queries were also directly called "topic queries plus evidence." This shorthand made communication easier, but compressed two unconfirmed relationships: whether topic and evidence always came from the same document identity, and whether evidence was always returned with the topic in the same way. The initial draft continued using this shorthand not because those relationships had been confirmed, but so the same group of people could quickly recognize the investigation record. The ambiguity it retained later fed back into the choice of entry point.

## Broader Investigation Paths Not Adopted

Some favored starting with claim source identifier and document identity, comparing the objects involved before and after topic hits. This path did not become the starting point. Initially, there was no reliable success/failure comparison, and expanding into object comparisons too early would likely produce a series of differences that could not be mapped to the text seen in the user's environment; the decision at the time was not to expand the reading scope to all claim, source, and document objects yet.

Another suggestion was to first capture all visible text from evidence-rich, then decide whether to read the implementation. This suggestion did not become the main path either. The old draft was concerned that collecting samples first would slow down localization, so it chose to read the code near the query first, then return to ask for additional results from the user's environment. As a result, proximity in the code path was given too much explanatory weight: a name being close to the terms used for the problem does not mean the file owns that behavior.

What was actually decided here was an order, not ownership of responsibility. First inspect where text is formed near the query; if that cannot explain the differences, expand the scope. The old draft did not clearly distinguish order from attribution, so some later cited it as a policy of "send evidence issues to the query side first." This reading is still retained alongside the original draft.

## Reading Entry Point

The old investigation notes point to `rag/advanced_rag/knowlege_compile/wiki_incremental.py`. This path is retained because the problem terms and call names once led readers here, not because it had been confirmed to handle all behavior of Evidence-rich topic queries.

At the top of the file, `from __future__ import annotations` is visible, along with `asyncio`, `json`, and `logging`. These establish only the nearby elements visible during one reading: there may be asynchronous flows, structured text processing, and logging. They do not individually prove which step produces topic, evidence, or the differences seen in the user's environment. The old record included this kind of proximity information in its basis for "query side," giving the impression that the available material was already sufficient.

The entry point's original purpose was narrow: after opening it, look for actual references linking topic, evidence, claim, source, and the visible results. It does not replace a pair of call results, nor does it replace confirmation of input conditions. Although the initial draft did not spell this out, there was no material supporting a further interpretation of the path as implementation ownership.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Seen
    Seen: Inconsistent topic query results
    Seen --> QueryFirst
    QueryFirst: First inspect near the topic query
    QueryFirst --> PairPending
    PairPending: Await saved visible results from success and failure
    PairPending --> [*]
```

The end in the diagram does not mean the problem was resolved; it only means the initial draft stopped here. It records the order adopted at the time: first enter near the query that produced the visible results, then wait for paired results, rather than a completed localization path.

## Incomplete Counterexample Collection

The initial draft requested that two results be retained: one successful call and one failed call, with the visible text for both topic and evidence saved together. The plan did not produce samples in the old draft, nor did it produce comparable fields, ordering, or document identifiers.

This gap directly affects the old judgment. Without paired outputs, it is impossible to confirm that "the topic is still there" refers to the same topic, or to confirm whether evidence is missing, shorter, reordered, or merely displayed in a different position. The old conclusion was not withdrawn because samples were missing; it simply remained on the page as a working assumption treated as supported by default.

Therefore, the follow-up action originally allowed should have been very narrow: after obtaining a pair of visible results, first compare the topic text and evidence text, then decide whether to continue tracing the objects along the path. The initial draft described this as a later follow-up, but did not make it a condition for attribution. This is the main reason the page is retained but is no longer suitable for citation as a current judgment.

## Later Card Review

The linked card ARG-216 later completed owner confirmation and moved into review after implementation was completed on an existing branch. What can be known here is that the card went through confirmation and a review request; these actions do not establish which old explanation was proven, nor can "completed on an existing branch" be read as meaning that the successful and failed results were fully reproduced.

ARG-216 remains the navigation point back to material from the user's environment. The to-do left in the card was to save the visible results from one successful call and one failed call separately. This to-do aligns with the gap in the old draft, but it did not supply the sample content missing from the old draft at the time.

The review also mentioned DOC-30. The two pages are adjacent only in navigation: DOC-30 handles Complete navigation graph text, while this page retains the old attribution for Evidence-rich topic queries. Both involve text or scope, but that does not justify transferring an explanation directly from one page to the other. The old draft did not make this distinction, and only later did a tendency emerge to misread "complete navigation" as a path for explaining evidence text.

The review did not fill in the original success/failure outputs, nor did it document the complete call relationships from topic to evidence for `wiki_incremental.py`. It only tightened how this old record should be read: the path remains an entry point for reading code, ARG-216 remains an entry point for material from the user's environment, and "query side first" remains the decision made at the time.

## Conclusions Still on the Page

The original decision has not been deleted: first investigate the visible output near the topic query, and only expand to evidence, claim source identifier, and document identity if the differences cannot be explained there. It was once used to control the investigation scope, and it also pushed call conditions and object relationships too far back too early.

This is not a complete account of evidence-rich behavior. It preserves only the trade-off decided at the time: choose a narrow entry point, accept the cost of incomplete counterexample collection, and defer broader object comparisons. If the two results required by ARG-216 are supplied later, they should first be placed where they are missing in this record, rather than directly expanding the old query-side judgment into a new attribution.

# Navigation Graph Text Proposal

Continue the discussion with a narrower assumption: Complete navigation graph text is not a concatenation of the few headings readable on the current page, but text that captures the navigation relationships for downstream inspection. The format we'd like to try in the first version puts the root title first, followed by descriptions of the entities in the graph; leave the exact separator and handling of empty descriptions undecided.

There are two candidate approaches. One is for the interface to return this text directly, giving the caller a complete result. The other is for the interface to retain only the navigation object and let the reader expand it into text. The first makes it easy to archive a single output; the second requires fewer changes to the existing object, but callers will each develop different ways to expand it.

# Navigation Graph Text Proposal

When we first investigated this, the leads pointed to `api/apps/services/dataset_api_service.py`. At the time, we didn't break down what "a complete navigation graph" meant: the root title appearing, the page looking readable, and the caller receiving a block of text were treated as the same thing. Keeping that simplification in the record is useful because it explains the initial preference for simply adding a block of text; it is not a suitable basis for evaluating the interface now.

> Earlier recommendation: the root title can stand in for the whole graph; entities with descriptions just need to be included in the text. Entities without descriptions can be left out of the output as long as readability is not affected.

The recommendation above is retained here, but is no longer the default approach for the trial. It mistook "readable" for "complete" and did not explain whether callers actually needed names, descriptions, or the relationship between the two. If two readers obtain different sets of entities from the same graph, a block of text that reads well is not enough to locate the discrepancy.

When we later checked the entry point, we could confirm that this file was an existing Python module, with direct imports of `logging`, `json`, `os`, and `re` at the top. That still makes it a suitable starting point for this follow-up investigation, but does not automatically validate the original output assumptions. Dependencies near the entry point might support request handling, serialization, or cleanup; interpreting them directly as steps for generating navigation text would conflate the file's location with its actual responsibilities.

This trial should narrow the question to three comparable candidates rather than commit to a final interface up front.

1. **The interface generates the full text.** The root title appears first, and entities in the graph are expanded along the existing navigation relationships; entity descriptions are part of the candidate content. The caller receives text that can be retained, suitable for checking a single generation result. The cost is that the interface must define the meaning of empty descriptions, repeated entities, and ordering.
2. **The interface returns a navigation object, and the reader generates the text.** The existing object shape takes priority, with text rules left to the caller. The trade-off is not simply less formatting logic to write: each readerFang Ke can independently decide which entities count as part of the graph.
3. **Provide only the root title and an entry point for further queries.** This option requires the fewest changes, but it cannot answer what complete means in "Complete navigation graph text," and could easily lead callers to mistake follow-up queries for output that is already complete.

The tentative recommendation is still to try the first option, but the reasoning has changed: not because a block of text is inherently more correct than a navigation object, but because it forces us to define the content scope explicitly. At a minimum, the trial output should let people identify where the root title and entity descriptions each come from. Whether entity names are retained separately and how entities without descriptions are represented should not be decided by how the display looks. An entity with only a name and no description is exactly the counterexample needed to challenge the earlier recommendation: omitting it makes the text shorter but may change the scope of the graph; retaining it requires an agreement that empty content does not mean a parsing failure.

The responsibility boundary here also needs to be narrowed. The service entry point can handle a generation or return operation, but "which entities are in the graph" cannot be decided implicitly by the text-formatting stage alone. If callers still need to trim the navigation object according to their own criteria, they should do so explicitly outside the interface, rather than first calling the result complete and then silently removing items from the text. Conversely, if the text is only a diagnostic byproduct, it should not define the meaning of the navigation object in turn.

ARG-217 contains a maintenance action: rerun the corresponding entry point on a platform supported by the maintainers, and check the files and versions actually generated. This takes priority over further discussion of naming. During the rerun, retain the locations where the root title, entity descriptions, and entities without descriptions each appear, so we can determine whether the first candidate really covers the required scope; merely checking whether the final page contains a block of text is not enough to distinguish the three candidates.

The withdrawal criteria have been revised into two categories. If the rerun shows that the existing entry point already produces stable, complete text, do not add a parallel output; only fill in the instructions for callers to use that result. If the result shows that the text comes from an ad hoc expansion by the reader, or that the generated files are unrelated to the expected entry point, withdraw the recommendation for "this interface to provide the full text directly," retain the navigation-object path, and compare again who should be responsible for expansion. Neither case should carry forward the earlier recommendation that "entities without descriptions can be skipped."

Still unresolved: whether entity order is part of the interface semantics; whether the same entity should be written repeatedly when it appears in multiple navigation relationships; whether the text can still be called complete when the root title is missing; and whether the files actually generated contain the same content as the object read by the caller. Before the rerun, these remain candidate choices, not established behavior.

# Caller Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

During integration testing, call samples from the same client were marked with different states at two entry points. Both records pointed to the current revision, but they were captured at different times; on later review, the last query result could not simply overwrite the earlier record.

The first discrepancy to surface was that the credential shape did not match the old record. As a result, the integration feedback could not establish which phase of the compatibility window the sample was in: one entry point still interpreted it according to the original adaptation boundary, while the other already showed a recoverable state. At the time, changes in adjacent services were not recorded as the cause.

## Timeline

- The initial capture preserved the state and request context at the time and revealed a credential shape different from the old sample.
- A subsequent recheck of the current entry point produced another record of the current revision. The two records were not merged into a single "latest state."
- Further retries were stopped. The original record was retained separately, and the recovery page did not overwrite it.
- Calls could later be resumed within the compatibility window; this only shows that the window could still handle that client, not why delimiter routing changed.

## Impact and Response

This affected sample assessment and integration feedback during caller integration testing; it was not a confirmed global service outage. Further requests would produce more mixed-together records, so the stop condition was to preserve the version, request context, and exit action first, then decide whether to run further checks.

After recovery, the old record remained the basis for assessing the state when the anomaly occurred, while the recovery page only described the entry-point state after recovery. The two coexisting states are not duplicates to delete outright during cleanup: they correspond to different capture times and preserve clues that the adaptation boundary changed.

The unresolved question is still why delimiter routing changed. The available material is insufficient to attribute it to the client or other services. Missing timestamps were not fabricated either; if shift records are found later, they should be placed alongside these two original records rather than used to rewrite the assessment made here at the time.

# Caller Exit Window Checklist

This page preserves the check sequence for one web-client-integration exit window. It was originally written for people about to close the window: preserve the state first, then decide whether to remove the temporary setup. The relevant owner must still sign off separately on whether the release succeeded; checking boxes on this list cannot replace that step.

The entry point is still at `docs/adj-web/release/web-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`. After opening the page, first confirm that you are looking at records for this window; do not bring in results from a similarly named client. Here, "last visible result" means a result that was already visible before the exit action, not a green result produced by a later rerun.

## What to Keep Before Opening the Window

- [ ] Write down the version of the entry point currently in use, and keep this run's client input with that version.
- [ ] Keep one success path and one rejection path. Continue using the old name `negative sample` for the rejection path; its purpose is to show that the rejection branch was actually reached at the time, not to require collecting every failure.
- [ ] Check whether `model discovery` has left a result. If there is no result, you can continue with partial checks, but you cannot mark the model discovery step as complete.
- [ ] If this window uses borrowed accounts, proxies, or other temporary access arrangements, note when they are to be removed before starting. Confirming other projects' schedules is not covered here.

The old version treated `atomic media` as a hard stop: without it, the window could not be closed. That rule is retained here because the records at the time were organized solely around it; it is not a required artifact for every later caller integration session. When reviewing an old window now, first check whether it actually appears in the final result for that input. If it does not, follow the stopping rule used at the time; do not fill the gap with output from an adjacent trial.

## Exit Actions

1. First stop new client requests from entering this window, then check the records already in the window for any new visible results. Do not remove the bypass while the queue is still accepting new work; otherwise, output produced after the window closes will get mixed into the samples from within the window.
2. Keep the last result together with the input and entry-point version. Keeping only the word "success" from the logs is not enough; at a minimum, it must be clear which client the result belongs to and whether it appeared before or after the exit action.
3. When checking `token budget`, look at the artifact or state itself. Earlier records used the success message in the logs as a substitute, which leads to an unpersisted state being incorrectly marked as complete.
4. If temporary diagnostics have changed the input, access arrangements, or processing path, mark that run's result as not comparable to results from the original setup. Do not use it to overwrite the samples kept earlier.
5. After the exit action is complete, remove the temporary permissions and bypass. If removal would leave requests still being processed without an entry point, stop before removal and preserve the state first; do not perform a partial rollback.

`credential shape`, `lossless split`, and `delimiter routing` are check labels that appeared on the old page. Use them for verification only when the corresponding records already use those labels; do not add checks to a new window just because they are listed on this page. In particular, do not treat the result of `lossless split` as proof that client requests can continue to run; those two points were not combined into a single conclusion in the old window either.

## Deciding Whether to Close the Window

- [ ] The last visible result has been retained and can be matched to this run's input.
- [ ] It has been confirmed that no new client requests will enter this window.
- [ ] Temporary permissions and the bypass have been removed, or removal has explicitly been halted and left incomplete.
- [ ] Name the actual person taking over each incomplete item; "the project team will continue to monitor it" does not count as handoff information.

If the second item is not met, stop before closing the window: retain the current input, version, and last result, and do not remove the bypass. If the third item is not met, do not mark the window as closed either; just record where removal is blocked. The recovery actions have not been tried in the shared environment to date; adding more checks later has not changed that.

`document identity` and `topic evidence` are only suitable for reviewing old material: the former helps distinguish pages with the same name, and the latter helps determine whether a result was recorded for the current topic. They do not constitute a release gate. DOC-35 contains the migration index for the current and old entry points; if you need to find an entry point, you can continue from there, but do not treat the migration status as the exit decision for this checklist.

This page is still preserved as a record of the old window. If the exit conditions change in the future, a separate record should be kept for the new window; do not turn this old checklist into a general release process.

## Entry Record

Before starting, find this round's materials through `docs/adj-harness/release/harness-quality-signal-exit-window-checklist.md` and record the version shown on the page. The final value displayed on the page is only a reference for locating the materials; keep the samples in their original chronological order.

- [ ] Save the original test input, the version used, and the first visible result.
- [ ] Keep one success sample and one rejection sample. They serve as references for this round's regression tiering, not as replacements for the failure context.
- [ ] Record the target of this round's exit action. "Handled" without a target is not a valid window closure record.
- [ ] If the materials come from an unfinished window in the previous round, mark the handoff point at the beginning. Do not renumber old samples as new results.

"First visible result" means the earliest saved result that shows the state of the test; it does not need to explain the cause. It may be a failure, or just a signal that has not yet stabilized. Without it, any subsequent recovery record has no baseline for comparison.

## When Deviations Occur During Processing

First check whether the deviation comes from the test context itself rather than the way the records were organized. If you change the test conditions, filtering scope, or recording method to investigate a problem, put the results after that change in a separate section. Do not paste them beneath the original failure sample and create the impression that two sets of conditions existed in a single run.

Stop the exit action immediately in any of the following cases:

1. The page version cannot be matched to the samples at hand;
2. The last visible result points to a different target from the original failure sample;
3. The recovery operation changed the test context, making it impossible to tell whether the signal changed because of recovery or because of the change;
4. There is only a verbal explanation, with no result that can be retained.

Stopping does not mean deleting records. First revert the temporary changes made for diagnosis, then place the before-revert and after-revert records alongside the original failure sample in chronological order. If no result appears after the revert, record that as unconfirmed too. Do not overwrite a failure in the original window with a later successful test; both must remain in the exit window for later regression tiering decisions.

## Window Closure Actions

- [ ] Check against the entry record and confirm that the exit action being closed out has actually stopped.
- [ ] Review the last visible result once more; it should be in the same record section as the saved version and target.
- [ ] Append recovery results after the original failure window without changing that window's target or order.
- [ ] Keep the original description of signals whose cause has not been reliably established. Do not treat "not reproduced so far" as a recovery conclusion.
- [ ] Return the release decision to the relevant owner. This checklist completes the exit record for adj-harness; it does not sign off on the release outcome on the owner's behalf.

An early draft required cleaning up the test context as soon as subsequent results became available. That no longer applies: cleanup loses the temporal relationship between the failure sample and recovery results. Keep the original sample and append records of the recovery actions instead. If a recovery action has not yet been verified, leave that gap in the record; do not fabricate results to close the window.

ARGC-005 noted that the page version might not match the chronology of the materials. When organizing this page, first put the test samples and exit actions in their original chronological order, then use the page's final value as supporting evidence. A newer page does not mean that every result on it occurred later.

This card is no longer used here to drive exit actions; it is retained only as a navigation aid. When taking over the work, still start with the checklist file and the saved samples.

ARGC-010 is linked to appending recovery results, not using them as replacements. If this round produces a recovery record, place it after the corresponding failure window and retain the original failure target. If no recovery record has been produced yet, the window closure record should explicitly stop at the last visible result. Work on this card has started, but that does not mean recovery is complete.

The person handling the handoff should be able to find at least the following in a single record: this round's original test input, version, first visible result, exit action, and whether any recovery record was added later. If any item is missing, do not broaden the interpretation. Leave unconfirmed points unresolved and stop the exit assessment on this page.

Even if the next round only reruns the same test, record its result separately. A rerun is not a revision to the original window; it is a new observation, and comparison is meaningful only while the original sample remains visible.

# Alternative Approach Proposal for Quality Signals

This page preserves an approach to organizing the material that was not adopted. It was not originally meant to replace harness · Quality Signal Board's entire workflow, but only to obtain both regression tiering and flaky-signal attribution while replaying existing failure samples. Material added later changed that premise, but the original proposal was not deleted; people still come here to check why it was not pursued at the time.

The working assumption in the original proposal was that replaying samples as-is could provide enough clues from the test to do two things in a single pass—place the failure in a regression tier and say whether it was a flaky signal. This assumption avoided extra recordkeeping and made early trials look straightforward. It treated "being able to reproduce a failure" and "being able to explain a failure" as too close to the same thing.

Two approaches were listed at the time.

- **Combined approach**: Use each resulting failure sample as the unit of replay, and record its regression tier and flaky-signal attribution within the same test. This avoids having to jump to another record when checking the sample, but the attribution will change along with that replay.
- **Separate approach**: A replay retains only the original sample and the test result; regression tiering and flaky-signal attribution are recorded separately. The two records can point to the same sample without requiring both to be established in a single replay.

The original proposal favored the combined approach only because it saved a step in organizing the material. At the time, there was not enough material to explain the role execution records played, nor was the handoff process considered part of the proposal. In hindsight, this is exactly why it should no longer be treated as implementation guidance.

The addendum first introduced a counterexample: the adjacent entry's then-current result was normal, while this record cut off before the execution record. This did not prove which stage the failure came from, but it was enough to invalidate the old simplifying assumption. Without an execution record, a replay can show that a sample had produced a failure, but that is not a basis for attributing the flaky signal to the execution process; a normal result from the adjacent entry cannot make up for the missing record either. The premise that "one replay can handle both tiering and attribution" therefore no longer held.

The requirement recorded in ARGC-008 also made the sample boundary clearer: replay the original harness-quality-signal; do not reconstruct a similar sample. This restriction was not meant to make the trial look more rigorous, but to prevent a newly created sample from conflating the original failure pattern with later judgments. Once the combined approach needs to create a similar sample to fill an attribution gap, it has already moved away from the object it claims to be comparing.

The supplemental handoff record for ARGC-013 still does not have all the details for who handed it off, who took it over, and the confirmation time. Although the handoff was later marked as confirmed, the missing fields still show that this approach cannot treat "someone has taken over" as evidence that the attribution is ready for review. The original proposal left no room for gaps like this: it accounted only for samples, tests, and classification results, not a situation where the execution record cut off first.

The withdrawal criteria for this approach were therefore defined more narrowly in a later update:

1. If a replay cannot continue to use the original failure sample, do not continue the comparison;
2. When the execution record is missing, do not record the flaky signal as attributable to execution;
3. If regression tiering must depend on an unconfirmed handoff record, keep the candidate tier, but do not incorporate it into the existing process;
4. If maintaining the combined approach requires reconstructing a similar test, withdraw the approach itself rather than treating the new sample as a substitute for the original.

This page does not conclude that "the separate approach is already in effect." Separate recordkeeping was only a point of comparison for the combined approach at the time, not an arrangement that had been put into practice; without complete execution records, it cannot produce complete attribution either. The old draft framed the two approaches as an efficiency trade-off. After the addendum, it reads more like a trade-off over record boundaries: the former saves a step in organizing the material, while the latter at least does not pass off replay results as an explanation of execution.

Two open items remain. First, which flaky signals can be kept as candidates based on the test alone, and which must wait for complete execution records before a judgment can be made; second, whether the mapping between the original replay and regression tiering needs to be rechecked after the supplemental handoff record is complete. Neither item is closed on this page.

To review the original proposal and attachments, start with `docs/adj-harness/proposals/unused-harness-quality-signal-board-approach.md`. DOC-40 documents another lookup path from the current entry point to the current revision; do not use the two pages interchangeably.

# Two-State Performance Experiment Postmortem

This incident centered on a very narrowly scoped object: the same object under rag · Performance Lab appeared in two states at different entry points. The lab still used capacity baselines, resource curves, and degradation localization to organize its day-to-day work; the anomaly did not automatically invalidate all of these materials. What changed was that, when readers traced the materials back from an entry point, they could no longer be sure that the two pages pointed to the same current record.

The initially retained material fell into two categories. One was the original record from when the discrepancy was first seen; the other was the recovery page that could later be opened again. They served different purposes. The original record preserved the evidence that "two states once existed"; the recovery page showed that at least one entry point later became accessible again. If only the recovery page were retained, it would later be impossible to tell where the states first diverged; if only the original record were retained, the recovery that happened later would be omitted.

## What Was Seen at the Time

| Stage | Observed situation | Action |
|---|---|---|
| First discovery | The same object appeared in two states | Preserve the original entry point and original record |
| Initial comparison | Two time points showed different current revisions | Do not designate either as the sole current state |
| Recovery page appears | One entry point became accessible again | List it separately as recovery; do not remove the old evidence |
| Investigation continues | No continuous record of the cause yet | Start from the generation information and look for the first divergence |

The "two states" were not merely two pieces of text that looked different. A matching name only shows that the reader entered the same work topic; the fact that a page opens only shows that the page was accessible at that time. To determine whether the two records actually describe the same result, at minimum the entry point, current revision, material generation time, and exit action must be considered together. Without any one of them, the comparison can easily be skewed by the page title or display format.

Capacity baselines, resource curves, and degradation localization are easy to mistake for the arbiter in this incident. They were originally used to describe capacity, resource changes, and where performance degradation occurred, and remain part of the lab object; but they cannot determine which record is current for an entry point. Even if a resource curve is still present, an entry point may still land on an old record. Conversely, even if an entry point has been retargeted, that does not establish that the resource curve has been regenerated or degradation localization recalculated.

The investigation therefore did not modify the capacity baseline as its first step. Changing the baseline first would have conflated normal experimental changes with this entry-point discrepancy. When the original record was reviewed afterward, it would then have been difficult to distinguish which changes came from the investigation and which were already present in the evidence. Resource curves were also not used as evidence of a fix: a curve reappearing could only show that another piece of material was available to view; it could not show why the old entry point had once pointed to another state.

## Original Hypothesis

An early hypothesis was that the old record might not have been unlinked from the entry point promptly. It seemed to explain why the recovery page later became available, but not why the two time points showed different current revisions or why the original record could still be found. The bigger issue is it did not specify which piece of material the exit action was actually associated with.

The hypothesis was kept, but it cannot be treated as the cause. Treating it directly as the cause would focus follow-up work only on the old page and overlook possible differences among the generation record, the post-export pointer, and the exit conditions. At this point, the appropriate wording is: misaligned record updates are an explanation still to be verified, not a confirmed conclusion.

Another approach that was not adopted was repeatedly refreshing the entry point and waiting for the two displays to become consistent on their own. That would leave more page copies from different times without necessarily adding any material that could explain the source of the divergence. The first point of difference was enough as the investigation starting point; without generation times and generation records, further retries would only make the evidence harder to organize.

## Comparison Scope

Subsequent comparison starts with the generation time of each of the two pieces of material. If the times differ to begin with, the two batches may have been mistakenly treated as a single batch; if the earlier portions match and the later portions begin to differ, only then should the generation process be traced further to find the divergence. The goal of the comparison is not to retell the lab's entire history, but to identify the earliest point that cannot be matched.

Next, check the current revision shown by the entry point. It is the direct trigger for this anomaly, but not the complete cause. Different revisions may appear at any stage of material generation, material export, or retargeting of the entry point. Simply labeling them "old" or "new" without considering their generation times cannot show where the difference occurred.

Check the exit action separately. The lab has separate exit conditions; page accessibility is not evidence that the exit action is complete. A restored entry point may still correspond to an old exit record; even if the exit action has been updated, the public entry point may not immediately show the same content. Both need to be retained; one cannot be used as a substitute for the other.

Only then revisit the capacity baseline, resource curves, and degradation localization. They are used to confirm that readers are still discussing the same lab object, not to adjudicate the state of the entry point. If these materials themselves also show another inconsistency, record it as a new anomaly rather than mixing it into this timeline.

## What Is Still Missing

There is no continuous state history between the original record and the recovery page. It is now possible to confirm the earliest discrepancy and a later page that was accessible, but not to infer from those endpoints how each intermediate step changed. The time when the recovery page appeared cannot stand in for the time when the two states became consistent again.

Another unconfirmed item is the process stage from which each of the two states entered the entry point. The records left after generation may have differed, or the export or entry-point target may have changed; the available material still cannot distinguish between these possibilities. For the next update, prioritize retaining the generation information, the two time points, and the first divergence; do not use page appearance as the basis for a determination.
